title: Arena lifecycle and cudaMallocAsync behavior — investigative notes
content:
Summary:
This note captures an experiment-driven investigation into unexpected OOMs and degraded utilization we observed on A100 clusters when serving Llama-2-13B variants under (seq_len=2048, batch=1..8) traffic. Hypothesis that led this doc: fragmentation is driven by arena lifecycle interactions between cudaMallocAsync arenas, stream-local caches, and our workspace pooling logic. cudaMallocAsync behavior changes across driver/runtime versions and can leave transient "dead" spans that look free to our allocator but are unusable for large contiguous requests.

Goals:
- Reproduce a high-confidence fragmentation scenario
- Capture allocator/driver traces that expose arena creation/destruction patterns
- Quantify effective fragmentation ratio and where slack appears
- Propose mitigations we can ship quickly and medium-term engineering work

Quick findings (top-level):
- cudaMallocAsync (CMA) creates per-stream arenas that are returned to the driver asynchronously; the driver may split/merge arenas lazily. Large contiguous requests (>= ~2GB) fail even when cumulative free across arenas >= request size.
- Observed fragmentation ratio (1 - largest_contiguous_free / total_free) hit 0.58 in worst-case test on A100-80GB with mixed batched workloads; this caused 1.5–2x effective memory pressure vs. a compact map.
- Our workspace pool currently allocates several differently sized buffers per request (KV cache + activation workspace + temp layer buffers) with fast path trying cudaMallocAsync for each. Interleaving of these allocations across streams amplifies arena scattering.
- Preallocating a single large workspace per worker (and sub-allocating inside host) substantially reduced fragmentation; gives a pragmatic mitigation path for Dedicated.

Reproduction steps (short):
1) Start serving runtime with model=llama-2-13b, batch pooling disabled, workspace_pool_size=dynamic (default), worker_count=8, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set to single A100-80GB.
2) Run mixed traffic generator: low-latency single examples (seq=2048) interleaved with synthetic batch=8 high-memory requests; use two client threads offset by 50ms to create stream interleaving.
3) Capture with: nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys_run --trace=cuda,osrt --sample=none --follow-fork none --backtrace none --capture-range=nvtx --duration 60s --env "NSYS_MONITORING=1" -- python3 bench_mixed_traffic.py
4) Collect driver logs: sudo dmesg | tail -n 200 and /var/log/nvidia-installer.log; also enable CUDA_LOG_LEVEL=info for runtime.

Diagnostic commands used:
- nsys status/profile for per-kernel timeline
- python script using pynvml to poll cudaMemGetInfo every 100ms and log free/total and largest_free_contiguous (via driver debug APIs where available)
- exported CMA debug: export CUDA_MALLOC_ASYNC_LOG=1 (only on patched runtimes); check NVIDIA driver logs for arena create/free messages.

Representative allocator trace (abridged):
- t=0   worker0 streamX: cudaMallocAsync(size=1.4G) -> arena#7 allocated@0x5600.. (ok)
- t=14  worker1 streamY: cudaMallocAsync(size=512M) -> arena#9 allocated@0x6a00.. (ok)
- t=42  worker0 streamX: cudaFreeAsync(ptr=0x5600..) -> arena#7 partially freed (free span 1.4G)
- t=47  worker2 streamZ: cudaMallocAsync(size=3.8G) -> FAIL: out-of-memory (largest_contig < 3.8G)
- t=49  driver: merge attempt for arena#7/#9 deferred by GC window (driver passive coalescing)
Notes: although total free across arenas ~5GB, largest_contig was ~1.6GB due to fragmentation and alignment restrictions.

Metrics snapshot from worst run (A100-80GB):
- total GPU memory: 81.3 GB
- resident (our process): 67.8 GB
- total_free: 13.5 GB
- largest_contiguous_free: 5.6 GB (fragmentation ratio = 0.587)
- number_of_arenas: 14
- active_streams: 28
- observed OOMs: 3 in 10 minutes

Root-cause analysis (working theory):
1) Arena granularity + stream-local caching: CMA allocates arenas per stream with internal freelists. When many small and medium allocations happen on different streams, freed spans remain local and do not become globally coalescible until GC/driver merges.
2) Alignment & internal binning: The driver aligns spans and places them into size classes; large contiguous requests require an appropriately sized free span. Small-ish frees produce multiple non-contiguous spans.
3) Worker-level workspace churn: Our per-request pattern creates multiple temporaries with different lifetimes. Interleaving across streams means free patterns are staggered and prevent contiguous accumulation.
4) Driver heuristics and version differences: observed that driver 525.x exhibited more aggressive coalescing than 535.x in our tests. (See linked_artifacts for the PR where we pinned runtime in a toy cluster.)

Short-term mitigations (low engineering cost):
- Prewarm and reserve: at worker startup, cudaMalloc a single large contiguous workspace (e.g., 24–40GB depending on model and config) and sub-allocate inside process. This removes dependence on CMA for large critical allocations. Pros: fast to implement; cons: ties up memory even when idle.
- Batch allocator aware scheduling: make scheduler collocate large workspace requests on same stream or serialize large contiguous allocations to avoid scattering.
- Fallback model variant: when largest_contig < threshold (e.g., 4GB), route requests to lower-memory variant (quantized) rather than triggering OOM.

Medium-term engineering work (higher effort):
- Custom arena manager: maintain our own pooled arenas with deterministic merging, with a background compaction thread that requests full-device allocations then remaps subregions. Requires careful DMA & driver interactions; risk with CMA semantics.
- Allocation batching: implement a batched allocation API where workspace pieces are allocated as a single cudaMallocAsync under a unified stream, then split — reduces cross-stream fragmentation.
- Eviction-friendly KV cache: change KV cache eviction policy to free large contiguous KV shards first to create coalescible spans. This is model/workload dependent.

Experiments run (short log):
- EXP-2025-02-11-A: baseline dynamic pool, driver 535.86: fragmentation ratio median 0.41, OOMs: 5/24h
- EXP-2025-02-13-B: prewarm 32GB workspace per worker: fragmentation ratio median 0.09, OOMs: 0/24h, 7% throughput higher due to fewer retries
- EXP-2025-02-17-C: pinned chunk + suballocator + driver 525.85: fragmentation ratio 0.04, stable; shows driver interaction matters less once our allocator controls large chunks

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How does MIG partitioning affect CMA arenas? Anecdotal tests show MIG+shared driver changes arena behavior; need controlled test matrix.
- Cost model for preallocating per-worker workspaces vs. capacity gains from fewer OOMs — run cluster-level billing simulation.
- Explore whether RDMA/p2p comms cause additional arena retention in multi-GPU layouts (we saw delayed frees when p2p enabled).
- Investigate kernel-level fragmentation measurement: can we surface largest contiguous free span via an exported driver metric or NVML extension?

Recommended immediate action for Platform:
1) Ship a guarded prewarm flag for Dedicated (default off) + operator doc explaining memory reservation tradeoffs.
2) Add runtime check that samples largest_contiguous_free on startup and logs a per-worker health metric exposed to Console. If < threshold, route traffic to a safe fallback.
3) Add a quick benchmark in our CI that runs the mixed-traffic scenario at small scale to detect regressions. Link to PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842

Appendix — debugging snippets and scripts:
- pynvml monitoring snippet (poll every 100ms)
  (see linked PR for script)
- nsys capture flags used above and how to extract timeline segments around cudaMallocAsync calls
- suggested NV driver versions matrix to test: 525.85, 535.86, 545.x (notes differ across minor releases)

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic; I prioritized mitigations that reduce customer impact quickly. Medium-term work should be tracked as a follow-up epic.
- Please add experiment links and additional traces to the Confluence page.

---
Drafted by Marco Nguyen on 2025-02-10; updated after follow-up experiments on 2025-02-28.
